\chapter{Open, Closed, In, Out}
\label{ch:ml-open-closed}
\hlchaptermodality{95}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can open and close a door, ask somebody else to, and say which side of it I am on.}

From cold: the two verbs, the asking ending they share with the first commands, and the pair a doorway divides.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[tuṟakkuka]{\ml{തുറക്കുക} (tuṟakkuka) — to open}

\label{lesson:ML-C95-thurakkuka}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{door}. You have been able to name it for a long time and have never been able to do anything to it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\textbf{\ml{തുറക്കുക}} — \emph{tuṟakkuka} — \textbf{to open.}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{ഞാൻ} \ml{വാതിൽ} \ml{തുറക്കുന്നു}.} — \emph{ñān vātil tuṟakkunnu} — \textquotedblleft{}I open the door.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Look at what the sentence asked of you. \textbf{Nothing new but the verb.} The doer in front, the thing in the middle, the verb at the end — and \textbf{\ml{വാതിൽ}} takes no ending, because it is a thing and not a person.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{തുറക്കുന്നു}} \emph{tuṟakkunnu} & opens \\
\textbf{\ml{തുറന്നു}} \emph{tuṟannu} & opened \\
\textbf{\ml{തുറക്കും}} \emph{tuṟakkuṁ} & will open \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{Two of those three you already knew how to build.} Present and future are the stem plus \emph{-unnu} or \emph{-uṁ}, exactly as they were on the first verbs you learned.

\textbf{The past is the one you have to be told}, and you were warned about this a long way back: the coming-verb's lesson said the past \emph{\textquotedblleft{}is not\textquotedblright{}} built that way, that its stem collapses, and that \textbf{no rule would have told you so.} Here it happens again — \textbf{\ml{തുറക്ക}-} shortens to \textbf{\ml{തുറ}-} before the ending.

Guessing from the present would give you the wrong word. That is not a new difficulty; it is \textbf{the same single difficulty Malayalam has}, arriving on schedule. Learn a verb's past and nothing else about it can catch you out.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{tuṟakkuka}
  \item \emph{ñān vātil tuṟakkunnu}
  \item the same sentence about yesterday
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \emph{to open}? (\textbf{\ml{തുറക്കുക}}.) Does the door take an ending after it? (\textbf{No} — it is a thing.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[aṭaykkuka]{\ml{അടയ്ക്കുക} (aṭaykkuka) — to close}

\label{lesson:ML-C95-adaykkuka}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{to open}. Then say \emph{listen} — the command form from your first commands.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\textbf{\ml{അടയ്ക്കുക}} — \emph{aṭaykkuka} — \textbf{to close.}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{ഞാൻ} \ml{വാതിൽ} \ml{അടയ്ക്കുന്നു}.} — \emph{ñān vātil aṭaykkunnu} — \textquotedblleft{}I close the door.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Same shape as the opening verb, and \textbf{\ml{വാതിൽ}} is the thing being closed, not the thing doing the closing.

\begin{cousinweb}
Now ask both of them as a request, using the ending you have had since the command chapter:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{തുറക്കൂ}} \emph{tuṟakkū} & open it \\
\textbf{\ml{അടയ്ക്കൂ}} \emph{aṭaykkū} & close it \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{That is the same ending as \ml{കേൾക്കൂ}.} One long \textbf{\ml{ൂ}} on the end turns a verb into something you can ask for, and it did not care which verb you handed it.

This is the form that goes on a sign, and it is the form you say at a door with your hands full.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{aṭaykkuka}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{tuṟakkū}, then \emph{aṭaykkū}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{vātil aṭaykkū}
  \item \emph{Look:} at the end of \textbf{\ml{കേൾക്കൂ}} and \textbf{\ml{അടയ്ക്കൂ}}, and find what they share
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \emph{to close}? (\textbf{\ml{അടയ്ക്കുക}}.) How do you ask somebody to do it? (\textbf{\ml{അടയ്ക്കൂ}} — the long ending.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[akattŭ]{\ml{അകത്ത്} (akattŭ) — inside}

\label{lesson:ML-C95-akathu-purathu}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{open it} and \emph{close it}. A door is worth opening because of what is on the other side of it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
Two words, and they are the two halves of the same line:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{അകത്ത്}} \emph{akattŭ} & inside \\
\textbf{\ml{പുറത്ത്}} \emph{puṟattŭ} & outside \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{ഞാൻ} \ml{അകത്ത്} \ml{ആണ്}.} — \emph{ñān akattŭ āṇŭ} — \textquotedblleft{}I am inside.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{Read the ends and not the fronts.} The two words end the same way as each other, and what differs is only the front — where the whole meaning sits. One opens onto a room, the other onto a street.

The chapter before this had a pair the other way round: \textbf{\ml{ഇന്ന്}} and \textbf{\ml{ഇന്നലെ}} shared their \emph{opening} and parted at the tail. Here the tail matches and the fronts part. \textbf{Both pairs are easy for the same reason} — one end holds still while you listen to the other.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{akattŭ}, then \emph{puṟattŭ}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ñān akattŭ āṇŭ}
  \item \emph{Say it:} the same sentence about being outside
  \item \emph{Look:} at the two words and say which part carries the difference
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Inside and outside? (\textbf{\ml{അകത്ത്}, \ml{പുറത്ത്}}.) Which part of the two words is doing the work? (\textbf{The front} — the ends match.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[tuṟakkukayuṁ aṭaykkukayuṁ enna ōrmma]{(open, closed, in, out) — from cold}

\label{lesson:ML-R95-open-closed-recall}



\begin{quote}
Close the lessons before this one. Say \emph{to open} and \emph{to close}, then ask somebody to do each.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: four words, and none of them needed a new rule}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{തുറക്കുക}} & to open \\
\textbf{\ml{അടയ്ക്കുക}} & to close \\
\textbf{\ml{തുറക്കൂ}} & open it \\
\textbf{\ml{അടയ്ക്കൂ}} & close it \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The asking form is \textbf{the ending you have had since \ml{കേൾക്കൂ}}, put on two verbs that had never seen it. The three tense endings came the same way, from a verb you learned long before these.

\textbf{Two words bought four forms}, because the endings were already yours.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{ഞാൻ} \ml{അകത്ത്} \ml{ആണ്}.} — I am inside.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{വാതിൽ} \ml{അടയ്ക്കൂ}.} — close the door.
\end{quote}

The door was named a long way back and nothing could be done to it or about it. Now it opens, it closes, and there are two sides of it you can name.

That is the ordinary shape of this stage: \textbf{the sentence was ready before the words were.} The arrangement, the tense endings, the asking ending and the bare object all came from chapters that had nothing to do with doors.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{tuṟakkuka} $\to$ \emph{tuṟakkū}
  \item \emph{aṭaykkuka} $\to$ \emph{aṭaykkū}
  \item \emph{vātil aṭaykkū}
  \item \emph{ñān akattŭ āṇŭ}
  \item which ending the asking form shares with a word from your first commands
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Open and close? (\textbf{\ml{തുറക്കുക}, \ml{അടയ്ക്കുക}}.) How do you ask for either? (\textbf{The long \ml{ൂ} on the end}.) Inside and outside? (\textbf{\ml{അകത്ത്}, \ml{പുറത്ത്}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
